data: Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (lead) — DLR + CNES (MASCOT lander) + NASA (DSN tracking, sample-curation partnership)

490 kg dry, ion-electric propulsion (4×μ10 thrusters) + chemical bipropellant + 1.6 m HGA. Onboard payload — Small Carry-on Impactor (SCI, 2.5 kg shaped charge), MASCOT lander (10 kg, DLR/CNES), 3× MINERVA-II rovers (~1 kg each), sample return capsule (16 kg, parachute reentry).

© JAXA / Hayabusa2 mission. Hayabusa2 launched 2014-12-03 from Tanegashima on a 3.5-year low-thrust ion-engine cruise to near-Earth asteroid (162173) Ryugu, with an Earth gravity assist on 2015-12-03 to phase the rendezvous. Arrival 2018-06-27 at 20 km hover distance. Surface operations 2018-2019 returned the first sustained close-up survey of a rubble-pile C-type asteroid (~1 km diameter, ~1.27 g/cm³ bulk density — implying ~50% porosity). Two touchdown-and-go sample collections (TD1 2019-02-22, TD2 2019-07-11) bracketed the SCI experiment (2019-04-05) which detonated a 2.5 kg copper-lined shaped charge to excavate a 14 m crater and expose fresh subsurface material for the second sample. The DLR/CNES MASCOT lander operated for 17 hours on the surface, and three MINERVA-II hoppers returned the first surface images from an asteroid. Sample-return capsule reentry over Woomera, Australia 2020-12-05 (UTC; recovered 2020-12-06 local/JST) delivered 5.4 g of pristine Ryugu material — the first asteroid sample with subsurface stratigraphy. The Hayabusa2 mothership departed for an extended mission: flyby of 98943 Torifune (2001 CC21) in 2026-07, then rendezvous with rapidly-rotating (1998 KY26) targeted for 2031-07.
Watanabe et al. (2019) — Ryugu shape + density first results (Science 364)
Yada et al. (2022) — preliminary Ryugu sample analysis (Nature Astronomy)

Tanegashima, Japan, 2014-12-03. JAXA's follow-up to the original Hayabusa, designed to bring back a larger, less-contaminated asteroid sample. Targets near-Earth asteroid 162173 Ryugu — a primitive C-type carbonaceous body that may preserve volatile organics from the early Solar System.

Closest approach 3,090 km on 2015-12-03. The Earth flyby raises the spacecraft's aphelion enough to reach Ryugu's slightly-larger heliocentric orbit. Ion engines (four xenon thrusters) handled the cruise propulsion, demonstrating Japan's electric propulsion lineage from Hayabusa 1.

Arrived at asteroid Ryugu on 2018-06-27. Held station at 20 km for 18 months of mapping. Deployed three rovers (MASCOT and two MINERVA-II hoppers) that landed on the surface and operated in Ryugu's gravity of about 1/80,000 g — the first rovers to hop across an asteroid. Two touchdown sampling operations followed, including one inside an artificial crater made by a copper impactor.

Sample capsule re-entered over Woomera, Australia, 2020-12-05 (UTC; recovered 2020-12-06 local/JST), parachuting down with 5.4 grams of Ryugu material — vastly exceeding the 0.1 g minimum. The mother spacecraft continued on an extended mission: flyby of 98943 Torifune (2001 CC21) in 2026-07, then rendezvous with asteroid 1998 KY26 planned for 2031-07. Ryugu samples already revealed amino acids and water-bearing minerals, supporting the asteroid-delivery model of early-Earth volatiles.
Second asteroid sample return (Ryugu, 2020); first artificial impact crater on an asteroid; first subsurface asteroid material returned to Earth
